units.title: Unit 25 — Sport
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 54–55 (PDF pages 58–59).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
learningObjectives: Choose do, play or go with common sports and activities.
Distinguish playing a sport from practising a specific skill or attending a class.
Describe competition, training, victories, results, records and anti-doping tests naturally.
Use accurate football collocations for game positions, fouls, substitution and penalties.

items.example: I do gymnastics at the sports centre twice a week.
items.note: Use do with gymnastics, not play.

items.example: My cousin has started to do judo after school.
items.note: Do is the usual verb for martial arts such as judo.

items.example: He does weightlifting to improve his strength.
items.note: This names a sport or training activity; do, not play, is the usual verb.

items.example: Our neighbours do aerobics every Tuesday evening.
items.note: Aerobics regularly combines with do; go to aerobics refers to attending a class.

items.example: I do yoga before work to relax.
items.note: Use do yoga for the activity; go to yoga may refer to attending a lesson.

items.example: The two athletes do wrestling at a local club.
items.note: Use do for this combat sport; a person can also wrestle.

items.example: We do circuit training at the gym on Fridays.
items.note: Circuit training combines with do, not make.

items.example: She does archery as a weekend hobby.
items.note: Do combines with archery when referring to the sport.

items.example: Several pupils do athletics in the summer term.
items.note: Athletics is a collective name for track and field events in British English.

items.example: Would you like to play badminton after lunch?
items.note: Play is conventional for this racket sport.

items.example: We sometimes play billiards at the club.
items.note: Play combines naturally with competitive table games.

items.example: My sister used to play hockey at university.
items.note: Use play for organised team games such as hockey.

items.pt: jogar bowls; praticar boliche de grama
items.example: The residents play bowls on the village green.
items.note: Bowls is a lawn game in British English, not the same as ten-pin bowling.

items.example: They play rugby every Saturday afternoon.
items.note: Rugby takes play, like football and cricket.

items.example: He learnt to play golf during his holiday.
items.note: Use play with golf even though players are not competing in teams.

items.example: We play table tennis in the break room.
items.note: Play is the usual verb with table tennis.

items.example: Many children play cricket in the park.
items.note: Use play with cricket, a bat-and-ball sport.

items.example: My friends play baseball in a local league.
items.note: Baseball commonly takes the verb play.

items.example: They play chess during their lunch break.
items.note: Board games normally combine with play.

items.example: We play darts at the community centre.
items.note: Use play, not do, with darts.

items.example: Our family likes to play cards on rainy days.
items.note: Play cards refers to card games generally.

items.example: My grandparents play dominoes after dinner.
items.note: Use play with dominoes as a game.

items.example: I rarely play computer games during the week.
items.note: The verb is play, not do, for games.

items.example: Shall we have a game of cards before we leave?
items.note: Have a game of cards and play a game of cards are both natural.

items.example: We go fishing by the lake in spring.
items.note: With leisure pursuits ending in -ing, go is often the natural verb.

items.example: They go skiing in the mountains each winter.
items.note: Say go skiing, not make skiing.

items.example: My colleagues go bowling once a month.
items.note: Go bowling is the usual activity expression.

items.example: I go cycling along the river at weekends.
items.note: Use go for the activity; ride a bike also works in everyday contexts.

items.example: The teenagers go skateboarding after school.
items.note: Go normally precedes skateboarding as a recreational activity.

items.example: We go surfing when the sea is calm enough.
items.note: Surfing typically combines with go.

items.example: She learnt to go snowboarding on her first winter trip.
items.note: Go snowboarding names taking part in the sport.

items.example: They plan to go hang-gliding near the coast.
items.note: This adventure sport is expressed with go.

items.example: I go climbing at the indoor wall each Thursday.
items.note: Go climbing describes the activity; climb also works as a verb.

items.example: We go hill walking whenever the weather is clear.
items.note: British English uses hill walking for walking in hilly countryside.

items.example: My parents go sailing in the summer.
items.note: Sailing commonly takes go.

items.example: I go jogging before breakfast on Sundays.
items.note: Go jogging describes exercise at a steady, usually gentle running pace.

items.example: The children go swimming after school.
items.note: The idiomatic phrase is go swimming, not do swimming.

items.example: I go to yoga on Wednesday evenings.
items.note: Go to yoga usually means attend a scheduled yoga class.

items.example: The coach asked us to do exercises before the match.
items.note: Exercises combine with do, not make; the meaning is individual exercises rather than sport generally.

items.example: The pupils do activities outdoors during the camp.
items.note: Do activities is natural; make activities is not normally used in this sense.

items.example: Their team hopes to win a match this weekend.
items.note: Win combines with match; the opposite is lose a match.

items.example: It is disappointing to lose a match in the final minute.
items.note: Lose is the opposite of win in competition.

items.example: The home side worked hard and seemed to deserve to win.
items.note: The phrase evaluates performance, even when the result is different.

items.pt: ser derrotado por uma margem pequena
items.example: The visitors were narrowly defeated in extra time.
items.note: Narrowly means by a small margin; narrowly beaten is an alternative.

items.example: The runners train hard for several months before the event.
items.note: Train hard refers to sustained practice and preparation.

items.example: You can enter a competition through the club website.
items.note: Enter a competition means officially participate; go in for is another expression.

items.example: Our rowing team decided to go in for a competition abroad.
items.note: Go in for can mean enter or take part in a contest.

items.pt: participar de uma sessão de treinamento
items.example: I attend a training session every Wednesday evening.
items.note: Attend emphasises being present at an organised session.

items.example: We do a training session before every tournament.
items.note: Do focuses on carrying out the training; attend focuses on being present.

items.example: The younger team put up a fight despite the difficult conditions.
items.note: Means resist strongly or make an effort against opponents, even if defeated.

items.example: She hopes to gain a place in the final round.
items.note: Gain a place and get a place mean secure a position or qualification.

items.example: The cyclist hopes to break a world record next year.
items.note: Break a record means exceed the previous best result.

items.example: The swimmer managed to set a new world record.
items.note: Set a record establishes a recognised new best performance.

items.example: The athlete became a world record holder at the age of nineteen.
items.note: Holder is someone who currently possesses the record.

items.example: The team will face fierce competition in the final.
items.note: Fierce competition is demanding and difficult to beat; come up against also fits.

items.example: We expect to come up against intense competition this season.
items.note: Come up against means encounter an opponent or obstacle; fierce is another modifier.

items.example: You need patience and practice to achieve your ambitions.
items.note: Achieve means successfully fulfil a goal, not simply have an ambition.

items.example: He was delighted to achieve a personal best in the race.
items.note: A personal best is an athlete's own best performance, not necessarily a record overall.

items.example: Finishing in under four minutes was a personal best for her.
items.note: Personal best can be used as a noun phrase.

items.example: Better technique can enhance your performance over time.
items.note: Enhance means improve; the unit also mentions prohibited drugs in sport.

items.example: Sporting authorities warn that some competitors take drugs to gain an unfair advantage.
items.note: In the anti-doping context, take drugs refers to using substances, often banned ones.

items.example: An athlete may be suspended if they fail a drugs test.
items.note: Fail means that a test detects a prohibited substance or another rule violation.

items.example: Competitors may have to take a drugs test after the final.
items.note: Take a test means undergo it; fail a test means receive an adverse result.

items.example: We are due to play a football match on Sunday.
items.note: Have a football match is also possible; play focuses on participation.

items.example: Our next fixture is a home match against the champions.
items.note: Home describes a match played at the team's own venue.

items.example: They face an away match on Thursday.
items.note: Away describes a match played at the opponent's venue.

items.pt: campo de casa; estádio do time mandante
items.example: The club recently renovated its home ground.
items.note: A team's usual venue, not the pitch of the away team.

items.example: She managed to score a goal in the second half.
items.note: Score is the natural verb for getting a goal in football.

items.example: The defender tried to tackle an opponent near the touchline.
items.note: A tackle is an attempt to take the ball; it must follow the game's rules.

items.example: The midfielder managed to take possession of the ball.
items.note: Means gain control of the ball; possession is not the same as scoring.

items.example: A careless challenge can foul an opponent and stop play.
items.note: Foul describes an action that breaks the rules against another player.

items.example: The referee had to blow the whistle before the free kick.
items.note: Blow is the natural verb for using a whistle in sport.

items.example: The captain was chosen to take a penalty.
items.note: Take a penalty means perform the penalty kick, not receive the punishment.

items.example: The defender stepped forward to take a free kick.
items.note: Free kick combines with take in football.

items.word: drop a player from the team
items.example: The manager may drop a player from the team after several poor matches.
items.note: Drop means omit a player from selection, not physically drop them.

items.example: The coach decided to bring on a substitute near the end.
items.note: Bring on means send a replacement player into the match.

items.pt: assumir a liderança; passar à frente no placar
items.example: The visitors managed to take the lead shortly before half-time.
items.note: In a match, take the lead means move into a winning position.

items.example: We sometimes go water skiing on the lake in summer.
items.note: Like go skiing, the activity takes go; this is confirmed by the correction exercise.

items.example: I practise a tennis serve with my coach every weekend.
items.note: Practise stresses repeated training of a particular skill, unlike play tennis.

items.example: The pair managed to set a record in their age group.
items.note: Set a record means establish a best result; the matching exercise uses this shorter pattern.

units.title: Unit 26 — Health and illness
units.source: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition); printed pages 56–57 (PDF pages 60–61).
units.bookTitle: English Collocations in Use — Intermediate (2nd Edition)
units.category: Leisure and lifestyle · health and illness
learningObjectives: Combine catch, contract, develop, suffer from, be diagnosed with and sustain with appropriate conditions or injuries.
Describe physical fitness and habitual exercise using natural verb–noun partnerships.
Distinguish intensity and seriousness when describing illness, symptoms and pain.
Use injured for people and damaged for objects and recognise formal health-related register.

items.example: I often catch a cold during the winter months.
items.note: Catch is an everyday verb for becoming ill with a cold.

items.example: Several colleagues caught the flu during the same week.
items.note: The flu is an informal name for influenza; say catch the flu, not catch flu.

items.pt: pegar um resfriamento; sentir-se mal por causa do frio
items.example: Take a warm coat so you do not catch a chill.
items.note: A traditional expression for feeling ill after exposure to cold; it does not establish a medical cause.

items.example: The report said that several patients caught pneumonia in hospital.
items.note: Catch is idiomatic for acquiring pneumonia, though pneumonia can have different causes.

items.example: Travellers should learn how to reduce the risk of contracting a disease.
items.note: Contract is more formal than catch or get for developing an infectious disease.

items.example: She contracted malaria while working overseas.
items.note: Contract is a formal verb used for infections; malaria is transmitted by infected mosquitoes.

items.example: He contracted typhoid during a trip and received treatment.
items.note: The formal verb contract is used with typhoid.

items.example: Researchers study why some people develop cancer.
items.note: Develop focuses on the onset of a condition, not the moment of diagnosis.

items.example: The article discussed people who develop breast cancer at a young age.
items.note: Develop commonly collocates with types of cancer.

items.example: Some people develop diabetes later in life.
items.note: Develop means begin to have a condition; it is not equivalent to catch.

items.example: People sometimes develop arthritis as they grow older.
items.note: Develop is natural for an illness that begins over time.

items.example: Her grandfather developed Alzheimer's disease in his seventies.
items.note: Use develop for the onset of this condition; British spelling uses Alzheimer's.

items.example: My neighbour has suffered from asthma since childhood.
items.note: Suffer from can describe the experience of a long-term condition; have asthma is neutral.

items.example: He suffers from hay fever every spring.
items.note: Hay fever is seasonal allergic rhinitis, not an infection.

items.example: She used to suffer from backache after long journeys.
items.note: Suffer from commonly combines with ongoing pain or conditions.

items.example: The child had an attack of asthma during the trip.
items.note: An attack means a sudden episode of symptoms.

items.word: have an attack of hay fever
items.pt: ter uma crise de rinite alérgica
items.example: I had an attack of hay fever while walking through the park.
items.note: The expression describes an episode of allergic symptoms.

items.example: Several passengers had an attack of diarrhoea during the journey.
items.note: An attack refers to an episode; have diarrhoea is simpler and more common.

items.example: People may be diagnosed with cancer after different kinds of tests.
items.note: Diagnosed with names the condition identified by a medical professional.

items.example: The patient was diagnosed with leukaemia after further tests.
items.note: Use be diagnosed with for a medical diagnosis; leukaemia is British spelling.

items.example: Some adults are diagnosed with autism later in life.
items.note: The verb refers to identification of a condition, not developing it at that time.

items.example: The cyclist sustained minor injuries in the fall.
items.note: Sustain is a formal verb for experiencing injuries.

items.example: Fortunately, no passengers sustained serious injuries.
items.note: Sustain is common in news and formal reporting of accidents.

items.example: The motorcyclist sustained head injuries in the collision.
items.note: This formal phrase indicates injuries affecting the head.

items.example: Several runners suffered injuries during the event.
items.note: Suffer injuries is an alternative to sustain injuries.

items.example: She wants to be in good shape before the hiking trip.
items.note: Good shape refers to general fitness or physical condition.

items.example: Many people take regular exercise to stay active.
items.note: Take exercise is natural in British English; do exercise is also possible.

items.example: Some adults prefer to take vigorous exercise outdoors.
items.note: Vigorous describes the intensity of physical activity.

items.example: We try to eat a balanced diet throughout the week.
items.note: Balanced refers to a suitable variety of foods and nutrients.

items.example: The school organises workshops about healthy eating.
items.note: Healthy eating is the practice of choosing a generally nutritious diet.

items.pt: seguir um programa de condicionamento físico
items.example: I follow a fitness programme designed by my trainer.
items.note: Follow means carry out a planned series of activities.

items.pt: manter-se fiel a um programa; seguir o plano
items.example: It can be difficult to stick to a programme when travelling.
items.note: Stick to stresses consistency rather than merely starting a plan.

items.example: Walking regularly helps my parents keep fit.
items.note: Keep fit means maintain physical fitness.

items.example: The charity offers support to people who are terminally ill.
items.note: Terminally ill describes an illness expected to cause death; it is a serious and sensitive expression.

items.example: The patient described excruciating pain in his shoulder.
items.note: Excruciating is a strong adjective for extremely severe pain.

items.example: She sought medical help because she had unbearable pain.
items.note: Unbearable pain is pain that is extremely difficult to tolerate.

items.example: The documentary follows a family coping with an incurable illness.
items.note: Incurable means there is no known cure, not that symptoms can never be managed.

items.pt: ocorrer com frequência na família; ter histórico familiar
items.example: Heart problems seem to run in the family.
items.note: A condition that runs in the family is common among relatives, sometimes for genetic reasons.

items.example: I had to take a day off to attend an appointment.
items.note: Take time off refers to being away from work or duties.

items.pt: um problema de saúde leve; um mal-estar sem gravidade
items.example: He stayed home because of a trivial ailment.
items.note: Trivial means minor or not serious; it may sound dismissive of someone's symptoms.

items.example: The clinic treats minor ailments as well as routine illnesses.
items.note: Minor emphasises a condition that is relatively mild.

items.example: Her employer gave her leave while she recovered from a serious illness.
items.note: Serious describes the gravity of the condition.

items.pt: uma doença que ameaça a vida
items.example: The hospital provides specialist care for people with a life-threatening illness.
items.note: Life-threatening means the condition could cause death, not necessarily that it will.

items.pt: extremamente doloroso; doloroso de forma aguda
items.example: The injury was acutely painful at first.
items.note: Acutely intensifies painful; it often suggests a sharp or intense experience.

items.example: The swelling made the joint intensely painful.
items.note: Intensely modifies the degree of pain.

items.pt: uma dor surda; dor contínua e pouco aguda
items.example: After the workout, I noticed a dull ache in my shoulder.
items.note: A dull ache is usually steady and less sharp than stabbing pain.

items.example: The doctor may prescribe tablets when appropriate.
items.note: A clinician prescribes a medicine; a pharmacy dispenses it.

items.example: Rest helped relieve the pain in her back.
items.note: Relieve the pain means make it less severe, not necessarily remove its cause.

items.example: The treatment helped alleviate the pain for a few hours.
items.note: Alleviate is slightly more formal than relieve.

items.example: My colleague was taken ill during the conference.
items.note: A conventional phrase for suddenly becoming ill; often appears in news reporting.

items.example: He had a heavy cold and chose to stay at home.
items.note: Heavy cold means a bad cold; the opposite in the unit is a slight cold.

items.example: I had a slight cold but felt better by Friday.
items.note: Slight signals relatively mild symptoms.

items.example: I went to bed early because I had a splitting headache.
items.note: Splitting is an emphatic modifier for headache.

items.example: She was in a good mood after hearing the results.
items.note: Mood describes a temporary emotional state; the unit uses the negative form.

items.example: Two players got injured during the match.
items.note: People get injured; objects get damaged.

items.example: The equipment could get damaged during transport.
items.note: Objects get damaged, whereas people get injured.

items.example: The travellers experienced an attack of diarrhoea after the meal.
items.note: A formal alternative to have an attack of diarrhoea in the exercise key.

items.example: Please tell the nurse if you are in pain.
items.note: Use be in pain for a general state; describe the location with pain in the back, for example.
